A 30% drop is a fact worth explaining. But "bike lanes caused it" is a claim about the *efficient cause*, and you have only a before–after on the same streets. That leaves several other causes unexamined.

First, what was the trend *before* the lanes? If injuries were already falling, or if the prior year was unusually high, the drop may be regression toward the mean — the chick’s heart beats before the wings form, but the beat does not cause the wings.

Second, what else changed on those streets? Traffic volume, speed enforcement, lighting, the mix of cyclists — any of these could be the *moving cause*. You need to know whether the lanes were put on streets that were already being calmed.

Third, how are injuries counted? Same reporting rules, same hospitals, same threshold for "injury"? A change in recording is a formal cause masquerading as an efficient one.

Fourth, twenty streets is a small sample for "for the most part" generalizations. Were they chosen because they were dangerous? That selects for a bounce-back.

What would satisfy me: a parallel set of comparable streets *without* lanes, tracked over the same years, with counts of cyclists (exposure) not just raw injuries. Then we can ask whether the *form* of the lane — separated, painted, shared — makes a difference, and whether the effect holds across different street kinds.

Without that, you have a correlation and a plausible story. Plausible is not the same as demonstrated.

A 30% drop on the same twenty streets the year after lanes were painted — that is an observation, not a demonstration. I would want to know what else changed.

Did the number of cyclists on those streets rise, fall, or stay the same? If fewer people rode, injuries drop even if risk per rider is unchanged. Was the previous year unusually bad — a cluster that drew the lanes in the first place? Regression toward the mean mimics a treatment effect. Did enforcement, lighting, speed limits, or reporting practices shift at the same time? Were nearby streets without new lanes tracked as a comparison?

My candles-and-aperture test worked because I could cover one candle and watch its spot vanish while the others stayed. Here the "candles" — exposure, behaviour, reporting — are not held still. You have a before and an after, but no arranged condition that isolates the lane itself.

What would satisfy me: counts of cyclists and injuries on the treated streets *and* on similar untreated streets, over several years before and after, with weather and policy changes recorded. Then we could see whether the injury *rate* per cyclist-kilometre moved differently on the two sets. Until then the 30% is a story, not a proof.

A 30% drop after the lanes went in — that's a fact worth noticing. But the move from "followed" to "because of" is where the trouble starts.

We see the lanes painted and the injuries fall. We never see the *power* that makes the one produce the other. That's not a quibble; it's the whole structure of causal reasoning. You've got a constant conjunction on twenty streets over one year. But twenty streets is a small sample, and one year is a short run. Did cycling volumes change? Did the city also lower speed limits, improve lighting, step up enforcement? Did a wet summer keep fair-weather riders home? Did the reporting threshold shift? Any of those would show up as the same conjunction.

The wise approach isn't to deny the lanes helped — they well might — but to proportion the claim to what the evidence actually rules out. If you can show the drop held across similar streets that *didn't* get lanes, or that it persisted when you control for exposure, then the conjunction starts looking less like coincidence. Until then, you've got a plausible guess dressed in numbers.

What else changed on those streets, or in the city, that year?

A 30% drop sounds promising, but I should want to know the natural history of those streets before I could rest easy. One year is a mere snapshot.

First, the variation: did all twenty streets show the same decline, or did some fall 60% while others rose? The awkward cases teach most. Were there control streets—similar roads without new lanes—tracked the same way? If injuries fell there too, the lanes may not be the cause.

Second, who is riding now? If the lanes attracted cautious riders who previously stayed off those roads, the injury *rate* per cyclist might not have changed, only the mix of people. I would write to the cycling clubs and the hospital clerks: ask them whether the *kinds* of injuries shifted—fewer doorings, more junction turns? The practitioners know the detail no summary table shows.

Third, what else altered that year? Traffic volumes, speed enforcement, a wet summer that kept fair-weather riders home? I once soaked seeds in salt water for weeks to test whether they could cross oceans; here the equivalent is to check whether the drop persists in year two, three, five, and whether it holds on the streets where lanes were *not* built.

Until I see the variation between streets, the counts per rider-kilometre, and the awkward streets that break the pattern, I could not argue the lanes *make* cycling safer—only that something changed on those twenty roads. What would satisfy me? A longer series, a comparison group, and the cyclists' own accounts of where they still feel unsafe.

Thirty percent fewer injuries on those twenty streets. And on the twenty comparable streets that got no bike lanes — what happened there? Did injuries fall, rise, stay flat?

You have a before-and-after on the treated streets. That is not a comparison. It is a story the city can tell itself. I want to know the denominator: injuries per mile ridden, per trip, per cyclist. If cycling volume on those streets dropped thirty-five percent because nervous riders still avoid them, your "thirty percent safer" is a mirage.

And the injuries that disappeared — did they move to parallel streets? Did the city change speed limits, enforcement, signal timing at the same time? You need a control group of similar streets, same period, same counting method, same exposure measure. Standardised forms. Published so anyone can check.

Show me that table. Then I will tell you whether the bike lane did it.

Thirty percent. One year. Twenty streets chosen — by whom, and why those twenty?

If the city picked streets where injuries had spiked, regression to the mean alone gives you a drop. If cycling volume fell on those streets because riders avoided construction, the rate per cyclist may not have changed. If they also lowered speed limits, added signals, or ran a safety campaign, the lane is only one thread in a bundle.

You need the denominator: cyclist-kilometres on those streets before and after. You need a comparison group — similar streets without lanes, tracked the same way. You need to know whether the *kind* of injury shifted (dooring vs. intersection vs. rear-end), because a lane protects against some and not others.

And you need the mechanism. Does the paint change driver behaviour, cyclist positioning, or both? Does it attract novice riders who would otherwise have stayed off the street, changing the risk pool?

An ideal type of "bike lane intervention" would isolate the physical separation from every concurrent policy. Your data does not. The 30% is a fact; the causal claim is a hypothesis. Treat it as one.

That's a before-after comparison on selected streets. It risks nothing.

If injuries had risen 30%, you'd have said: traffic volume increased, or reporting changed, or it's regression to the mean — the streets were chosen *because* they had bad years. The theory "bike lanes improve safety" forbids nothing. Adler would have loved it.

What would refute the claim? A proper test needs a bold prediction made *before* the data: "On these 20 streets, injuries will fall by at least X% compared to 20 matched control streets with no lanes, after adjusting for cycling volume." Then you look. If the difference isn't there, the conjecture takes a hit.

Do you have exposure data? Were the control streets chosen in advance? Was the 30% figure predicted, or noticed afterward?

That's the kind of "textbook" inference that makes me uneasy. You have a before-after comparison on 20 streets with no control group, no exposure data, and a single year of follow-up. In the framework of traffic safety epidemiology, that's not a puzzle-solution — it's barely a puzzle.

What would make this coherent as evidence? If you showed me that the 20 streets were chosen because they had unusually high injury rates the year before, I'd expect regression toward the mean to explain most of the drop. If cycling volume fell on those streets — because confident riders moved there while nervous ones avoided construction, or because the lanes displaced traffic — the injury *rate* per cyclist might not have changed at all. If the city also lowered speed limits or added enforcement simultaneously, the lanes become a confounded variable.

The Aristotle move: what framework would make a 30% drop *not* mean "lanes work"? A framework where safety is produced by system-level interactions — volume, speed, intersection design, driver expectation — not by a single countermeasure. In that framework, your 20 streets are an uncontrolled experiment in a system that's already shifting.

What would satisfy me? A comparison group of similar streets without lanes, tracked over the same period. Exposure data — cyclist counts before and after. A pre-specified analysis plan so you're not choosing the metric that works. And enough years to see whether the effect persists or decays as behavior adapts.

Without those, you have a plausible story, not a result. Plausible stories are how normal science *starts*, not how it *concludes*.

That's a thin reed to lean on. Before I'd say bike lanes caused the drop, I'd want to know how those 20 streets were chosen. Did the city pick the ones with the worst injury records? If so, regression to the mean alone gives you a drop — the "ant on the beach" problem: the pattern may be in the selection, not the intervention.

Also: did cycling volume change? If fewer people rode those streets, injuries fall even if risk per ride stayed flat. Were other changes made at the same time — speed limits, enforcement, lighting? Did reporting practices shift?

The decision *process* that selected the streets is part of the evidence. Tell me how the city actually decided, and what else moved at the same time.

That's a tempting number, but I'd want to know what actually happened on those streets before I'd use it as evidence.

Who put the lanes in — was it a top-down decision or did neighbourhood groups push for them? Were they physically separated or just paint? Did enforcement change at the same time? Did cycling volumes go up, down, or stay flat? A 30% drop could mean fewer cyclists, not safer cycling per rider. It could be regression to the mean if those streets were chosen because they'd had a bad year.

I'd also ask: who monitors the lanes now? In the irrigation systems I studied, the farmers who made the rules also walked the ditches to see who was taking extra water. If the city painted lanes but nobody watches whether drivers park in them, the rule exists only on paper.

Show me the before-and-after counts, the design details, and what the cyclists and drivers themselves say changed. Then we can talk about whether the lane *caused* the drop or whether something else did.

First we must distinguish what each measures. Traffic counts record what people *do*; surveys record what they *say* they do, or think they do. I would trust the counts for the primary question—did car use fall?—for the same reason I watched the chick in the egg day by day rather than asking the hen: the phenomenon itself is the better witness.

But counts alone leave the *why* opaque. Did drivers switch to the bus, or did they stop making the trip, or did new residents arrive without cars? A survey can catch the final cause—the purposes that moved people—if the questions are framed to avoid the answers people think you want. People are poor observers of their own habits; they will tell you they "mostly take the bus" while the sensor counts their car every weekday.

So: use counts to settle the *that*, and a carefully designed survey—administered before and after, with travel diaries rather than recall—to approach the *why*. And watch the development over time, not just a before/after snapshot; the order in which changes appear tells you what matters to the organism, in this case the commuter.

Traffic counts. They are the spots of light on the wall: you see what actually passes. A survey is a person telling you what they *think* they did, or what they wish they had done. People misremember, they answer as they think they should, they conflate yesterday with last month. The eye is harmed by bright light, so something enters it — but the tongue is not so constrained.

But a count alone does not tell you *why* the number changed. The candle experiment worked because I covered one candle and watched its spot vanish. You need the analogue: a comparable street without the new bus route, counted at the same hours, in the same season. If the control street is steady and yours drops, the bus route has a claim. If both drop, look elsewhere — fuel price, a factory closing, a new ring road.

And if you also run the survey, treat it as a second instrument: check a sample of respondents against fare‑card data or anonymised phone traces. Where the two agree, you have something. Where they diverge, ask which instrument is misreading the phenomenon.

What does the control street look like in your setting?

Traffic counts, and it isn't close.

A survey asks people what they *say* they do, or what they *remember* doing, or what they *think* they ought to have done. You know how that goes. A man tells you he walks to work three days a week; you watch the road and his car is there every morning. The testimony is sincere, perhaps, but it passes through memory, vanity, and a desire to please the interviewer. I spent enough time weighing human testimony against uniform experience to trust the road over the respondent.

Traffic counts give you the thing itself: metal passing a point. They have their own flaws — a tube across the lane doesn't know whether the driver *would* have taken the bus if the service were reliable, or whether she simply moved house. But they don't lie about what happened yesterday.

If you can, watch the same road before and after the route opens, and watch a similar road where nothing changed. That's the closest you'll get to a constant conjunction. The survey might tell you *why* people changed, which the tubes cannot. But for *whether* they changed, count the cars.

A survey asks people what they *say* they do; traffic counts show what they *actually* do. I should trust the counts more, for the same reason I distrusted a breeder's boast about his pigeons until I measured the birds myself.

But — and this is the awkward part — counts alone miss *who* changed and *why*. A survey catches the man who drives Monday–Wednesday but takes the bus Thursday when his wife needs the car. The counter sees only one car fewer on Thursday.

If I were doing it, I would want both, taken together, and I would look hardest at the days where they disagree. That disagreement is the variation that tells you something real. I would also want counts before the route opened, not just after — otherwise you have no baseline, only a snapshot.

And I would go stand at a bus stop myself, notebook in hand, at 7 a.m. and 5 p.m., for a week. There is no substitute for watching the thing happen.

Traffic counts. People misremember, misreport, and tell you what they think you want to hear. A sensor on the road doesn't.

But a count alone tells you nothing about *who* stopped driving or *why*. You need the before-and-after on the same road, same days, same hours — and a comparable road where no bus started, to net out the background trend. That's your control. Without it, you'll credit the bus for a recession, a fuel price spike, or a wet summer.

If you can afford it, add a small travel diary *sample* — not a survey — to see whether the same people switched modes or whether new people appeared. But the count is your mortality table. The diary is your hospital case notes. You need the table first.

What's your baseline period, and have you picked a control corridor?

Traffic counts tell you what happened. A survey tells you what people say happened, and perhaps why they think it happened. They answer different questions.

If you want to know whether car volumes dropped on the corridor, count the cars. But a count alone cannot attribute the change to the bus route — petrol prices, a factory closure, a wet summer all leave the same trace. You would need a control road, or a before/after series long enough to see the noise.

If you want to know whether the bus route *caused* the change for the people who switched, you must ask them — or better, watch a few of them closely. A survey gives you motives, but people misremember, rationalise, and tell you what they think you want to hear. The gap between reported and actual behaviour is itself a finding.

My instinct: start with the counts to see if there is an effect worth explaining. Then use a small, well-designed survey (or interviews) to test *which* mechanism operated — cost, time, reliability, habit break. The ideal type of "rational mode choice" rarely matches the messy reality; the deviation is where the explanation lives.

What is the decision you need to inform? That shapes which error you can afford.

Traffic counts. They measure what people *do*, not what they say they do. A survey can be reconciled with almost any outcome — people over-report virtue, samples skew, questions lead. If car counts on the relevant corridors don't drop, your conjecture ("the bus route reduced car use") has failed a test it could have failed. That's what makes the test severe.

But — and this is where it gets interesting — a traffic count alone doesn't tell you *why* the number moved. Fuel prices, a new employer, roadworks, weather. If counts fall, you haven't yet shown the bus route caused it. You've only shown the effect you predicted *might* happen did happen. The next step is to rule out the alternatives. That's where a *well-designed* survey helps: not as a substitute for counts, but as a probe for mechanism. "Did you switch because of the new route?" If the counts drop *and* switchers cite the route, you've survived a tougher test.

So: start with counts. They're the risky prediction. Use the survey to interrogate the mechanism, not to measure the effect. What would make you abandon the claim if the counts don't budge?

Not my territory — I studied physics and the history of the physical sciences, not transportation research. But the question you're asking is familiar in structure.

You're not choosing between a "biased" and an "unbiased" measure. You're choosing between two different operationalizations of "car use," each embedded in a different way of seeing the problem. Traffic counts give you flow at specific points, on specific days, with no information about who is driving or why. Surveys give you self-reported behavior, subject to recall error and social desirability bias, but they can tell you about mode substitution, trip purpose, and equity effects.

In the fields I know, the community's shared exemplars — the model problem-solutions students work through — settle which measurements count as legitimate for which questions. What do the exemplary studies in *your* field do? If the best-regarded evaluations of transit interventions use both, triangulating, then that's the disciplinary matrix speaking. If they privilege one, ask what anomalies the other measure keeps missing.

I'd want to know: what would count as an anomaly for each measure? If traffic counts don't budge but surveys show mode shift, what does your framework say happened? If they disagree, which puzzle do you try to solve first?

Traffic counts. People are terrible witnesses to their own routines. They'll tell you what they *think* they do, or what they *wish* they did, or what they did last Tuesday because it was raining. A pneumatic tube across the pavement doesn't have an aspiration level.

But — what decision are you trying to inform? If the city needs to know whether to keep the route funded, a 12% drop in peak-hour volume on the parallel arterial might be all you need. If you need to know *who* switched so you can design the next route, counts won't tell you that. A survey might, if you ask about specific trips ("how did you get to work last Thursday?") not general habits ("do you usually drive?").

The ant on the beach: the complexity you see in the data comes mostly from the environment — weather, school calendars, gas prices, that construction project on Main. Before you attribute a change to the bus, you need a baseline that captures the beach. Two weeks of counts before and after won't cut it. You need the seasonal pattern.

So: start with continuous counts on the arterial and the bus itself. If they move in opposite directions at the right times, that's your first answer. Then, *if* you need the "why" or the "who," add a targeted travel diary — not a retrospective survey — on a representative sample. Each method answers a different question. Don't let the budget decide the method; let the decision decide.

That depends entirely on what decision you're trying to inform and who needs to be convinced.

Traffic counts tell you what happened to vehicle volumes on the measured links. They won't tell you whether the same drivers switched to the bus, whether new trips appeared, or whether traffic just displaced to parallel streets. If the city council needs to know "did congestion ease on Main Street?", counts help. If the transit agency needs to know "did we attract new riders from cars?", counts alone can't answer.

A survey can capture mode shift at the household level — *if* you catch people before and after, and *if* they answer honestly. But recall is poor, social desirability bias is real, and response rates for travel surveys have been dropping for decades.

What I'd want to know first: what's the institutional setting? Who has authority to act on the results? In the water basins I studied, the producers themselves needed evidence they could trust *collectively* — so they built monitoring they jointly owned. Here, if the transit agency and the road department answer to different bosses, they may distrust each other's data. The method has to be credible to the people who have to agree on what to do next.

Have you talked to the decision-makers about what evidence would actually move them?

You're comparing two different things and calling them the same. Town A counts near-misses one way (an app makes it trivial), Town B another (no app, so only the memorable or dangerous ones get reported). The cycle paths in Town B might reduce actual near-misses, or they might just shift where they happen. You can't tell from these numbers.

First we must distinguish: are you trying to learn which town is safer for cyclists, or which reporting system captures more events? The app is an efficient cause of *reports*. The cycle paths might be a cause of *fewer actual conflicts*. But you have no common measure of the underlying phenomenon.

What would satisfy me: put the same reporting mechanism in both towns for a year. Or station observers at comparable junctions in each. Short of that, you have opinions, not knowledge. The numbers you have are "for the most part" noise.

The raw count tells you little. You have two confounded causes: the app makes reporting easy, and the cycle paths may change the actual danger. The reports mix what happens with what gets recorded—like judging the brightness of stars by how many names astronomers have written down for them.

If you want the actual rate, you need a measure that does not depend on the app. Station observers at comparable junctions in both towns for the same hours, count near-misses by a fixed rule, and see what they find. Or fit the same simple reporting device in both places—a paper form at a bike shop, say—and compare those returns.

Until you have a count gathered the same way in both towns, you only know that Town A produces more reports. You do not know which town is safer.

A familiar sort of puzzle. You're looking at the reports, not the near-misses themselves. The app is a new cause of reports; the cycle paths may be a cause of fewer actual incidents, or they may just move the conflicts where no one sees them. You have two different mechanisms producing the numbers, and you're trying to read a single fact — "which town is safer?" — from their combined output.

It's like judging which kitchen has more mice by counting mousetraps. One housewife sets traps diligently; the other has a cat. The trap count tells you about the housewife, not the mice.

What would help? If Town A's app existed last year, compare its own reports over time. If Town B gets an app, watch what happens to its numbers. Absent that, you're guessing at the hidden causes from the visible effects — exactly the place where custom masquerades as reason.

That is a classic trap. You are comparing two different filters, not two realities.

Town A's app *creates* its own reports. Anyone with a phone, a grievance, and the app installed can log a near-miss in seconds. Town B has no such funnel — so its cyclists either say nothing, call a council number nobody answers, or complain at the pub. The raw count tells you more about the reporting apparatus than about the streets.

The cycle paths in Town B are a separate variable. They may genuinely reduce conflicts, or they may shift them to junctions where paths end. You cannot tell from the numbers you have.

What would satisfy me: find the *same* observer in both towns. Station a careful person at a dozen comparable junctions in each — same hours, same weather, same definition of "near-miss" — and let them count with a clicker for a month. That is the salt-water seed experiment: test the awkward step yourself.

Failing that, ask the cyclists. Write to the local cycling groups in both towns with a short, identical questionnaire: "In the last month, how many times did a car pass you close enough to startle you? Where? Time of day?" Treat their knowledge as evidence. You will learn more from fifty riders' notebooks than from two aggregated dashboards.

And always, *always* ask: what would the data look like if the true danger were *equal* in both towns? The app would still show more for Town A. That thought experiment is your control.

You have two different counting systems measuring two different things, and you're trying to compare the raw outputs. That tells you nothing about relative safety.

Town A's app lowers the friction of reporting. Town B's cycle paths may lower the actual hazard. You have no denominator — no exposure data (cyclist-kilometres, junction crossings, time on road) — and no common case definition. A "near-miss" in the app may be a close pass; in Town B it may be whatever a cyclist bothers to tell a councilor about.

If you want to know which town is safer for cyclists, you need:
1. Comparable exposure measures in both towns.
2. A standard definition of "near-miss" applied by the same method (or at least calibrated methods) in both.
3. Ideally, injury and fatality counts too — harder to miss, harder to game, and the outcome that ultimately matters.

Until then, the only honest statement is: "Town A generates more reports because it built a tool to generate reports. Town B built cycle paths. We do not know which intervention reduced harm."

What data do you actually have access to?

You have a measurement problem that looks like a substantive finding. The "reported near-misses" in Town A are not a count of dangerous encounters; they are a count of *acts of reporting* made possible by an app. In Town B the same encounters may happen — perhaps more, perhaps fewer — but they leave no trace in your data because the instrument for recording them does not exist.

This is exactly the trap I encountered with Offenbacher's Baden statistics: Protestants appeared over-represented among business owners and technical students. The figures were real; the question was what they *meant*. I had to ask what motives, conventions, and opportunities stood between the social fact and the statistical record.

Here you have two distinct causal chains. In Town A: near-miss → cyclist notices app → decides to report → record appears. In Town B: near-miss → cyclist has no easy channel → no record. The cycle paths may reduce actual risk, or they may shift it to intersections, or they may be irrelevant to the reporting gap. You cannot tell from the reports alone.

What you *can* say: the app creates a new kind of meaningful action (reporting) with its own selection effects — younger cyclists, smartphone owners, people with time and motivation. Town B's silence is not evidence of safety. It is evidence of *no reporting apparatus*. If you want to compare danger, you need a measure that does not depend on a tool one town lacks.

The raw count tells you almost nothing about which town is safer. You have two confounding differences at once: a reporting mechanism that *creates* data in Town A, and infrastructure that might *prevent* incidents in Town B.

Ask what would refute the claim "Town A is more dangerous." If you removed the app from Town A and the reports dropped to near zero, the claim collapses — the difference was an artifact of visibility, not risk. That's the severe test: does the theory survive when you take away the instrument that produced the evidence?

The cycle paths are a separate conjecture: "more segregated infrastructure reduces near-misses." But you can't test it with this comparison because the measurement systems aren't comparable. It's like judging two hospitals by death rates when one only admits critical cases.

What's your actual problem? If it's "where should I build cycle paths?", you need a design that holds reporting constant — same app in both towns, or matched police reports, or observational studies. If it's "does the app work?", roll it out in Town B and see if reports rise while incidents (measured independently) don't.

First, decide which conjecture you're trying to break. Then build a test that could break it.

That comparison is nearly useless as it stands. You're measuring two different things with two different instruments in two different environments.

The app in Town A *creates* its own data. Before it existed, those near-misses still happened — they just weren't counted. Town B has no equivalent instrument, so its count is a floor, not a ceiling. Meanwhile, twice the cycle paths in Town B doesn't just mean "safer" — it means cyclists and cars are separated differently, so the *occasions* for near-misses change. You can't treat the raw numbers as comparable any more than you could compare thermometer readings from a mercury bulb and an infrared sensor without knowing their calibration.

What would interest me: what does each town *count* as a near-miss? Does the app define it? Do cyclists in Town B even have a concept of "reportable near-miss" without a channel? The anomaly isn't the rate difference — it's the assumption that the two numbers live in the same measurement space.

If you want to learn something, you'd need to understand the reporting *practices* in each town, not just the outputs. How many cyclists? How many trips? What does a cyclist in Town B do when a car passes too close — shrug, complain to a friend, call a non-existent number? That's where the history of the phenomenon lives.

That's the ant on the beach. The path looks complicated—more reports in Town A—but the complexity is mostly the beach: the app makes reporting trivial, so you get data. Town B has no easy channel, so near-misses vanish into silence. The raw counts tell you about reporting systems, not safety.

What decision are you trying to make? If it's "where to invest in infrastructure," you need a measure that isn't hostage to who built an app. Hospital records, insurance claims, a matched survey of cyclists in both towns—something with a common denominator. Or run a controlled before/after when Town B gets an app.

The cycle paths in Town B are interesting. They're a structural intervention. If you want to know whether they work, compare near-miss rates *on streets with and without paths* within Town B, using the same reporting method (or none). That's a nearer-to-decomposable comparison.

First question I'd ask: what would you do differently if Town A turned out to have twice the *actual* near-miss rate versus half? If the answer is the same—build more protected paths—then the measurement problem is secondary. If the answer changes, you need a better yardstick.

That's a measurement problem dressed up as a safety problem. You're comparing reported near-misses, not actual near-misses. The app in Town A creates a reporting institution — low friction, visible, maybe even gamified. Town B's cyclists might have no easy way to report, or they might call a non-emergency line that nobody tracks.

First question I'd ask: what happens *after* a report in Town A? Does the city actually change intersections, adjust signal timing, send a letter to the driver? If reports go into a black hole, the app becomes theatre. In the irrigation systems I studied, the rule wasn't "report violations" — it was "the water master walks the ditch every morning and fines you on the spot." Monitoring and sanctioning were coupled.

Second: do the cycle paths in Town B actually separate cars and bikes, or are they painted gutters that drivers park in? Design matters. A path that dumps you into a busy roundabout creates its own near-misses.

Third: who rides in each town? If Town A's app attracts confident commuters who ride in traffic, and Town B's paths attract families who'd never ride otherwise, you're comparing different populations facing different risks.

Go talk to the cyclists in both towns. Ask them where they feel unsafe and what they do about it. The data you have tells you about reporting institutions, not safety.

First, we must distinguish what happened. Did the pupils *choose* to use the app, or were they assigned to it? If they chose, the ones who used it may already have been more motivated, had more help at home, or simply liked reading more. That is not the app causing the gain; it is the kind of pupil who uses the app.

If they were assigned—some given the app, some not—then we can ask whether the groups were alike beforehand. Were they matched on prior reading scores, on language spoken at home, on whether someone reads with them? If not, the difference at the end may have been there at the start.

Also: what does the app actually *do*? Does it read aloud, give feedback, offer choices? The formal cause matters—what makes it a "reading app" rather than a game with words? And the final cause: is it meant to build fluency, vocabulary, comprehension? The test at the end must match what the app is for.

Show me the design. Was there a pre-test? A control group doing something else for the same time? Without those, we have a correlation and a plausible story, not a demonstration of cause.

That is a correlation, not a test. You say "pupils who used" — did they choose the app, or were they assigned? If they chose, then whatever made them choose (parents who read to them, prior ability, quiet homes) may be what raised the scores.

In my darkened room I set several candles before an aperture. Each cast its own spot on the far wall. Cover one candle and its spot vanishes. That arrangement *shows* light travels in straight lines; it does not merely correlate with it.

To argue the app improves reading, you need an arrangement where the only systematic difference is the app. Assign pupils at random: some get the app, some get a comparable activity (another app, extra books, extra time with a teacher). Keep conditions alike — same teachers, same home support as far as you can. Then measure. If the app group gains more, you have something to argue with.

Without that, you have a plausible story, not a demonstration. What would it take to arrange such a test?

A familiar puzzle. You've watched one ball strike another and the second move — app use, then higher scores — and you're ready to call it cause. But look at the table: the children who chose the app, or whose parents pressed it on them, likely differ in a dozen ways before the first swipe. More books at home? Parents who read aloud? Quieter evenings? Prior ability? You're seeing the second ball move and calling the contact the power, when the power may have been set in motion months earlier.

If the pupils were *assigned* by lot — some to the app, some to nothing — and the app group still pulled ahead, the conjunction grows more suggestive. But even then, you're trusting that the future resembles the past, which no logic guarantees. We believe it because nature has habituated us to, not because reason compels it.

What would satisfy me? Show me the randomisation. Show me the groups matched on the obvious confounders. Show me the effect surviving when you control for the things that *could* have moved the second ball on their own. And even then, speak of probability, not proof. A wise person proportions belief to the evidence, and the evidence here is still being gathered.

That is the sort of pattern that makes me reach for my notebook and then pause. Higher scores among app users — yes, but *which* pupils used the app, and were they already different before they opened it?

If the children who chose (or were given) the app had more books at home, more adult help, or simply enjoyed reading more to begin with, the app may be a marker rather than a maker. The awkward cases are the ones that matter: pupils who used the app faithfully and did *not* improve, and pupils who never touched it and improved anyway. Have you looked at those?

If you can find a setting where similar pupils were separated only by access to the app (a lottery, a phased rollout, a school that adopted it while a neighbour did not), that would be the analogue of my salt-water seed trials: a test of the awkward step.

What do you know about how pupils came to use the app in the first place?

That's not an argument. It's an observation with a leap in it.

Who used the app? Children whose parents downloaded it, made time for it, had devices and quiet spaces. Children who were already read to, or already liked reading. You've compared two groups that were different before the app existed.

Show me the same children before they used it. Show me children like them who *didn't* use it — matched on prior reading score, parent education, books in the home, language spoken. Then show me the difference.

Better: randomise. Give the app to half a class, not the other half. Measure both at start and end.

If you can't randomise, find a natural break — a school that rolled it out year by year, a cutoff date for access. Compare children just either side.

And tell me: what does "used" mean? Ten minutes a week? An hour a day? You need the dose, not just the label.

I spent years showing that soldiers died of filth, not war, because I compared soldiers to civilians of the same age in the same towns. The comparison did the work. What's your comparison that removes the excuse?

That is a correlation. You want a causal claim. The gap between them is where the work lives.

Who uses the app at home? Pupils whose parents already read to them, who have quiet space, who treat literacy as a family practice. The app may be a *symptom* of that environment, not its cause. You have an elective affinity between a certain kind of home and both the app use and the test scores. Until you can show what happens when you introduce the app into homes that *don't* already have that affinity — or at least account for why the affinity exists — you have not explained the result. You have only documented a pattern.

What would a comparison look like that lets you separate the app from the home?

That's a correlation, not a test. The pupils who chose to use the app — or whose parents made them — are already different. More motivated, more supported, better readers to begin with. Your "theory" (the app helps) explains the higher scores, but so does the rival theory (selection). A theory that fits both outcomes forbids nothing.

What would refute the claim? A severe test: random assignment, or a prediction that fails if the app is useless. For instance — if the app works, pupils who *started* behind but used it heavily should catch up faster than similar pupils who didn't. If they don't, the claim takes a hit. One awkward case doesn't kill a statistical hypothesis, but a reproducible zero-effect in a well-designed trial would.

Show me the risky prediction you staked, and the test that could have falsified it. Otherwise you're piling up confirmations — exactly what Adler did.

That's a correlation. You want a causal claim. The gap between them is where most educational interventions go to die.

What do you know about the pupils who *didn't* use the app? Or the ones who started and stopped? If the app-users had parents who read to them, or quieter homes, or better baseline vocabulary, the app gets credit for what the household already provided. That's not a methodological quibble — it's the difference between a puzzle that fits the current framework and an anomaly that might force a new one.

In the physical sciences we'd ask: what would a failed prediction look like? Here, a controlled trial with null results. Do those exist? Have you looked for them, or only for the positive correlational studies? The community's shared exemplars — what counts as convincing evidence in reading research — matter more than your single study's p-value.

Show me the design that would let a skeptic say "alright, the app did it." Not "what supports my claim." What would *falsify* it?

That's a correlation, not a causal claim. The question is: who chose to use the app, and what else differs about them?

In Milwaukee I watched recreation managers allocate budgets. They didn't optimize across departments; each pursued its own goals with the information it had. Families choosing a reading app are doing the same. Parents who download it likely value reading already, have more books at home, read with their kids, or have more flexible schedules. The app may be a signal, not a cause.

Before arguing the app improves reading, I'd want to know the selection mechanism. Was assignment random? Was there a waitlist? Did the app roll out in some schools first? If not, you're comparing two self-selected groups. The "effect" you see may be the environment — the beach, not the ant.

What does the data actually tell you about *how* the decision to use the app was made?

That's a correlation, not a causal claim. The pupils who used the app at home — who are they? Whose decision was it? Kids whose parents push reading, or who already like reading, will use the app *and* score higher. The app might do nothing.

In the West Basin groundwater case, the producers who organised didn't just "happen" to have stable water levels. They built rules, monitoring, graduated sanctions. I'd ask: what's the *institution* around this app? Is use assigned, encouraged, voluntary? Who sees the data? What happens when a kid stops using it? If it's purely voluntary home use, you've got selection all the way down.

If you want to argue the app improves reading, you need a design that breaks the selection — random assignment, a discontinuity, something. Or you study the *variation* in how it's used: some teachers monitor, some don't; some parents get alerts, some don't. Compare those. That's the kind of comparison that tells you whether the *rules* around the tool matter.

What's the actual setting?

That depends on what you mean by "learned more." You need to say what kind of learning the method aims to produce before you can choose a measure.

If the method teaches pupils to recall facts or execute procedures under time pressure, a well-made test captures that directly. It gives you a common scale across many pupils. But a test score is a single number; it does not tell you *how* the pupil solved the problem, whether they understand why the procedure works, or whether they can transfer it to a new situation.

Teacher observations can catch those things — a pupil explaining their reasoning, catching their own mistake, applying an idea in an unfamiliar context. But observations vary with the teacher's attention, their prior expectations, and the moments they happen to notice. They do not give you a common scale.

In the *History of Animals* I recorded the chick's heart beating on the third day, the veins on the fourth, the feathers later. One kind of observation told me the sequence; another told me the structure. I needed both, and I needed to know what each was good for.

So: what does the new method claim to change? If it claims deeper understanding, you will need observations — structured ones, with a shared rubric, not casual impressions. If it claims fluency with a defined body of knowledge, the test may suffice. If it claims both, you need both, and you need to say in advance what pattern across the two would count as confirmation.

A fair question, and one I would not settle by choosing either authority. A test score is an instrument; a teacher's observation is a report. Both mix what is given with what is inferred.

With my refraction apparatus I measured angles in air, water, glass — case by case — before I trusted any rule drawn from them. I would do the same here. Take pupils you *know* have learned (and some you know have not), by some independent sign — perhaps they can solve a new problem of the same kind without help. Then see which measure tracks that known ground. Does the test score rise only for those who can do the new problem? Does the teacher's note? If the test rewards memorised steps but not transfer, it is measuring the wrong thing. If the teacher sees effort and calls it understanding, that is inference, not sensation.

Neither is trustworthy until checked against a case where the answer is already visible. Arrange that check first.

A sensible question, though the phrasing "which would you trust" suggests you want one oracle instead of two fallible witnesses. I'd want to know what each actually shows you.

Test scores: you see a number on a page, produced under known conditions, marked by a known scheme. The impressions are uniform and repeatable. If the same pupil sits the same paper twice, the scores tend to cluster. That's a strong constant conjunction. But the number only tells you how the pupil performed on *that* paper on *that* day. The leap from "score rose" to "learning increased" is an inference, not an observation.

Teacher observations: the teacher sees the pupil across weeks, tasks, moods, conversations. The impressions are richer but far less uniform. One teacher notices what another misses; the same teacher weighs evidence differently on a tired Friday. The conjunction between "teacher says improved" and "pupil actually improved" is real but variable.

If you force me to choose for a *specific* purpose: for comparing groups at scale, the scores give you a steadier measure. For understanding *how* a pupil is thinking, the teacher's accumulated view carries evidence no score captures.

The wise course: use both, note where they agree and where they diverge, and proportion your conclusion to the weight of each. Neither gives you the "power" connecting method to learning—only constant conjunctions, some tighter than others.

Not my territory, but the question is familiar in form: what does each measure actually capture, and what slips through?

Test scores give you a number, comparable across classrooms. But they measure what the test writer thought mattered, on one day, under pressure. A pupil who understands but freezes, or who guesses well, both distort the figure. You get a snapshot, not the growth.

Teacher observations catch the halting explanation that suddenly clears, the question that shows real curiosity, the persistence on a hard problem. But they vary with the teacher's attention, memory, and tacit standards. Two teachers watching the same child may write different accounts.

If I were forced to choose, I'd want the observations *recorded systematically*—not impressions at term's end, but notes made weekly on specific behaviours: "pupil asked for harder text," "explained fraction to peer," "gave up after two tries." Then I could compare across teachers and see whether the pattern holds.

Better still: both, but treated as different species of evidence. The test shows whether the measurable knowledge shifted. The observations show *how* the pupil engages with the material over time. The awkward cases—pupils who score well but show no curiosity, or who struggle on tests but ask the sharpest questions—are the ones that tell you whether the method is doing what you hope.

What does the new method actually ask pupils to *do*? That should shape what you watch for.

Neither, on its own. You have the same problem I had with army returns: surgeons recorded "wounds" and "disease" in ways that made comparison impossible, and the categories themselves hid what was killing men.

Teacher observations are not standardised. One teacher's "engaged" is another's "distracted." You cannot compare classrooms, let alone schools, unless the categories are defined, taught, and checked the way William Farr and I forced the Army Medical Department to define theirs.

Test scores are standardised — but they measure only what the test captures. If your new method teaches reasoning, collaboration, or persistence, a multiple-choice paper will miss it, just as counting only battle wounds missed the cholera and typhus that killed nine men for every one hit by a Russian bullet.

What I would do: define the outcomes you actually care about — *before* you choose instruments. Then build or choose measures that capture each outcome, administered the same way, at the same times, by people trained to the same rubric. If that means a structured observation protocol *and* a validated test *and* samples of pupil work scored blind — use all three. But each must be comparable across every classroom in the study.

Otherwise you are not measuring learning. You are recording impressions.

That depends entirely on what you mean by "learned more" — and whose meaning you are trying to capture.

Test scores give you a standardised, comparable measure of certain performances. They are an *ideal type* of measurement: deliberate, abstract, useful for comparing across classrooms or years. But they tell you nothing about what the pupil *understands* the material to mean, or whether they can use it when the format changes. A score is a trace, not the thing itself.

Teacher observations catch something different: the hesitations, the sudden connections, the moments a concept becomes a tool for the child. That is *Verstehen* — interpretive understanding of meaningful action. But it is not comparable across teachers, and it is shaped by the teacher's own expectations, biases, and implicit theories of what "learning" looks like.

If your question is *whether the method raises average performance on a defined domain*, scores are the proper instrument. If your question is *how the method changes the quality of pupils' engagement with the material*, observations are indispensable — provided you treat them as data to be interpreted, not as transparent windows.

The mistake is to ask which source is "more trustworthy." Each is trustworthy for a different question. Decide the question first.

Neither. Or rather: the question is backwards.

You don't choose a measure because it's "objective" or "rich." You choose it because your theory makes a **risky prediction** that this measure could falsify.

What does the new method *forbid*? If it claims "pupils will score higher on the national maths exam," then test scores are your severe test — a null result refutes it. If it claims "pupils will develop deeper conceptual flexibility that standard exams miss," then existing test scores are the wrong test; they'd let the theory survive a failure it should have suffered. You'd need a new instrument designed to catch that specific claim — and you'd have to specify in advance what pattern of results would count as a refutation.

Teacher observations? They're theory-laden and flexible. A teacher who believes in the method will *see* confirmation; one who doubts it will *see* chaos. That's the Adler problem: the same classroom episode gets explained either way. Unless you blind the observers to the condition and pre-register the specific behaviours that would count as disconfirmation, observations are not a test — they're a Rorschach.

So: state the conjecture boldly. Say what it rules out. *Then* pick the measure that would most hurt it if it's wrong.

Not my territory — I studied physics and its history, not education research. But the question sounds like it assumes "learning" is a single thing both measures try to capture. In my terms, that assumes a shared paradigm that may not exist.

Test scores come from an exemplar that prizes standardization, comparability, narrow but sharp definition. Teacher observations come from an exemplar that prizes context, holistic judgment, the tacit knowledge a practitioner develops. They're not two instruments measuring the same quantity; they're instruments embedded in different problem-solving traditions.

Which do you trust? Depends on what puzzle you're trying to solve within which research tradition. If your community's exemplars treat learning as a latent trait measurable across classrooms, you'll trust scores — and you'll treat teacher variation as noise. If your exemplars treat learning as situated, emergent in particular relationships, you'll trust observations — and you'll treat standardization as distortion.

The deeper question: does education research have a disciplinary matrix stable enough that this choice gets made by shared commitments, or is it still pre-paradigmatic, where the choice *is* the debate?

That's the wrong first question. The right one: **what decision are you trying to make?**

If you're deciding whether to adopt the method district-wide, you need a measure that aggregates reliably across classrooms and resists gaming. A standardized test — flawed as it is — gives you a common metric. Teacher observations don't aggregate; each teacher sees different things, uses different standards, and nobody checks their reliability.

If you're deciding how to help *this* pupil tomorrow, the test score is nearly useless. It arrives too late, covers too little, and tells you nothing about *why* the child is stuck. The teacher's observation — "she freezes on multi-step problems but talks through them if I sit beside her" — is actionable.

The deeper point: both are proxies. The real variable is the pupil's changed capability. You can't see it directly. A test samples it; a teacher infers it from daily contact. Each misses different things. Tests miss persistence, collaboration, metacognition. Teachers miss what they don't expect to see, and they're susceptible to halo effects.

So: **match the measure to the decision.** And if the decision matters, use both — but don't pretend they're measuring the same thing. They're two different lenses on a complicated object.

What decision are *you* facing?

Not my territory — I studied irrigation systems and police departments, not classrooms. But the question you're asking is the one I always asked: *what are you trying to see, and who's in a position to see it?*

Test scores tell you something narrow and comparable. Teacher observations tell you something rich and contextual. If the new method is meant to change how pupils *think*, not just what they recall, a score sheet won't catch it. If you need to know whether the method spreads across schools, you need something comparable.

In the water basins I studied, the engineers had flow meters; the farmers had eyes on the ditches. You needed both, and you needed to know which one the users trusted when they made decisions.

If the answer is "the district decides whether to fund expansion," you'll need something the district can compare across classrooms.

And have you asked the teachers what *they* look for? In the Philippine zanjeras, the irrigators' own records were better than the agency's forms. Sometimes the users' measures are the ones that actually govern the system.

The reporting difference could reflect a difference in *permission to speak*, not in the underlying condition.

This is like studying chick development: if you only count heartbeats after day three, you miss the first pulse on day two. The instrument shapes what appears.

This is exactly the kind of tangle I would want to untangle by arranging conditions, not by arguing from the reports alone.

The wellbeing programme at School A may be doing two different things: changing how much anxiety pupils *feel*, and changing how readily they *name and report* what they feel. For instance: absence rates, visits to the nurse, observable avoidance behaviours, or a simple physiological indicator taken under the same conditions in both schools. Even a crude one — resting heart rate measured at the same time of day, same posture — would give me something independent of the reporting framework each school has built.

I would also want to know what the same pupils reported *before* the programme began, and before streaming was introduced. Without a baseline, the comparison is like judging the size of two objects by the shadows they cast under different lamps.

What can you actually measure in both schools that does not pass through the pupil's own judgement?

That's a fine puzzle. You have two schools, two different practices, and a difference in reported anxiety. The temptation is to read the correlation as causation: the wellbeing programme *causes* anxiety, or streaming *suppresses* it. But you only see the conjunction, not the connection.

Let me put it in terms I know. A boy strikes a ball; the second moves. We see contact and motion. We never see the "power" that makes the second ball move. Here you see School A's programme and higher reports. You don't see whether the programme makes pupils more anxious, or merely more willing to say so, or whether School B's streaming makes pupils quieter about it, or whether the schools differed before either policy began.

A few questions I'd want settled before I'd hazard a guess:

1. **Same measure, same moment?** If School A's pupils have spent a year practising the vocabulary of feelings, they may report "anxiety" where School B's pupils would say "nervous" or "stressed" or nothing at all. The impression has changed; the idea copied from it changes with it.

2. **Selection.** Did pupils choose the schools, or were they assigned? If parents of anxious children seek out the wellbeing programme, the causality runs the other way.

3. **What else differs?** Size, catchment, teacher turnover, exam pressure — any of these could be the real cause, with the policies mere accompaniments.

4. **Longitudinal data.** If you tracked the same pupils before and after the programme's introduction, you'd have a better shot at seeing whether the reports rise *because* of the programme or simply *with* it.

Without that, you have a plausible story, not evidence. And plausible stories are what the mind produces when custom fills the gap where reason cannot reach.

What do you actually have in the way of data?

That comparison troubles me exactly the way a field naturalist's notebook troubles me when two populations look different but live under different regimes. You have two confounded differences at once: the wellbeing programme *and* the streaming, and you have a measure—self-reported anxiety—that the programme itself teaches pupils to notice and name.

If a pigeon fancier told me his birds showed more "nervous temperament" after he started handling them daily and talking to them about their feelings, I'd want to know: did the birds change, or did his eye change? And if his neighbour's birds, sorted into high and low performers from week one, showed less "nervousness," I'd ask whether the sorting itself removed the birds that would have shown it—either by driving them out or by giving the remainder a predictable place.

What would satisfy me? Not a snapshot. I'd want the history of each cohort: anxiety reports *before* the programme started, and before streaming began, tracked term by term. I'd want the pupils who left each school—where did they go, and what did they report? Selection acts on who remains. And I'd write to the teachers who run the programme and the teachers who stream, asking precise questions: what do you actually *do* each week? Which pupils stop coming to the wellbeing sessions? Which pupils get moved between streams?

The awkward case is the pupil who reports high anxiety in School A *because* the programme gave them language for what they already felt, while a similar pupil in School B says nothing because streaming taught them their place is fixed. That case would not show up in your aggregate numbers.

Not my territory, but the logic is the same: never trust a difference between groups until you know the history of the individuals inside them.

That comparison as it stands tells you almost nothing about which school is "worse" for anxiety. You've got two differences at once: a wellbeing programme *and* streaming, plus whatever differences existed at intake.

Three questions I'd put before any conclusion:

1. **What were the pupils like before they arrived?** If School A takes children from more disadvantaged backgrounds, or with higher baseline anxiety, the raw scores reflect intake, not the programme. You need the same categories measured the same way at entry — or at least a credible proxy.

2. **Does the wellbeing programme itself increase *reporting*?** Giving children language and permission to name anxiety will raise reported rates even if actual distress is unchanged or falling. That's not a flaw in the programme; it's a measurement change. Did you measure the same constructs with the same instrument at the same time of year under the same anonymity conditions?

3. **What does streaming do to reporting?** Streaming may suppress expression — pupils in lower sets learn not to complain, or higher-set pupils mask distress. The comparison may be between "anxiety made visible" and "anxiety driven underground."

If you want to know whether the wellbeing programme *reduces* anxiety, you need a before-and-after in the same school, or a matched comparison where the only systematic difference is the programme. If you want to know whether streaming *increases* it, same logic.

What decision hangs on this? If it's "should we adopt School A's programme?", the answer isn't in the cross-sectional gap.

This is a textbook case of what happens when you treat a self-report as a transparent window onto a pre-existing state, instead of asking what the *institution* does to the very categories in which pupils experience and name their distress.

At School A, the wellbeing programme does not merely "measure" anxiety; it *constitutes* a vocabulary, a legitimate space, and a moral script for speaking about feelings. Pupils learn that anxiety is a recognised object, that naming it is virtuous, that the school wants to hear it. The report rises partly because the *meaning* of reporting has changed: it is no longer a complaint or a weakness but a participation in the school's own pedagogical ritual.

At School B, streaming by ability produces its own acute anxieties — fear of demotion, shame of the lower set, the quiet terror of the top set who must not fall. But the institution offers no authorised language for them. They may somaticise, withdraw, act out, or simply tick "not anxious" on a questionnaire because the category does not fit what they feel.

You have not found that School A *has* more anxiety. You have found that School A *produces more reports of anxiety* — and that is a different finding, requiring a different explanation.

What would satisfy me: treat the questionnaire not as a thermometer but as a document of the school's own regime of self-formation. Compare what each school makes *sayable* and *un-sayable*. Then ask whether the wellbeing programme, for all its unintended inflation of the metric, actually equips pupils to handle distress better than streaming equips them to suppress it. That is a causal question worth pursuing — but only after you have done the interpretive work.

That's not a finding, it's a tangle. You have two schools differing in at least two major ways — a wellbeing programme *and* streaming — and one outcome measured by self-report. Any of these could be driving the difference:

- The programme makes anxiety more visible (pupils learn to name it).
- The programme *causes* anxiety (endless talking about feelings).
- Streaming suppresses reporting (high-stream pupils hide it, low-stream pupils learn helplessness).
- Streaming actually reduces anxiety (clear expectations, less ambiguity).
- The schools differ in intake, catchment, leadership, a hundred other things.

You need a **risky prediction** that separates these. For instance: if the programme increases *reporting* but not *anxiety*, you'd expect physiological markers (cortisol, heart-rate variability) to show no difference — or even lower stress in School A. If streaming suppresses reporting, anonymous behavioural measures (avoidance, absenteeism, self-harm referrals) should be *higher* in School B despite lower self-report.

What would **refute** your leading conjecture? Say it out loud. Then design the test most likely to break it.

That's not a comparison. It's a category mistake dressed up as data.

You have two different worlds. School A teaches pupils that interior states are objects of scrutiny, named, discussed, tracked. Of course they report more anxiety — they've been given a vocabulary and a sanctioned occasion to use it. School B sorts pupils by measured ability; the salient categories there are "top set," "bottom set," "falling behind." You're treating "anxiety" as a neutral quantity like temperature, but the thermometer is part of the system being measured. That's the Aristotle moment: the term means different things inside different disciplinary matrices.

What would interest me: the history. How did each school arrive at its framework? What problems were they trying to solve? What exemplars — model interventions, past crises — shaped the staff's judgment about what counts as a wellbeing issue? Until you reconstruct those local grammars, your numbers are just cross-talk.

That's a classic "ant on the beach" situation. The complexity you're seeing may live mostly in the schools' environments, not in the pupils' underlying anxiety.

School A's programme *changes the measurement instrument*. When you encourage talking about feelings, you give pupils vocabulary and permission to report anxiety that School B's pupils might feel but not name. School B's streaming creates its own reporting norms—pupils in lower streams may suppress anxiety (stigma), while top-stream pupils may feel pressure they don't label as anxiety.

Two questions that would satisfy me:

1. **What's the selection story?** Are these comparable populations, or do anxious families choose School A *because* of the wellbeing programme? That's not a confounder—it's the premise of the organisation shaping who arrives.

2. **Do you have behavioural traces that don't rely on self-report?** Absenteeism, nurse visits, counsellor referrals, teacher ratings. If School A's pupils report more anxiety but show *fewer* avoidance behaviours, the programme might be working—making anxiety discussable and therefore manageable.

The streaming at School B is its own intervention. It sorts pupils into different task environments. A pupil in a lower stream faces a different "beach" than one in a higher stream. Aggregating across streams may hide more than it reveals.

What data do you actually have?

That's a measurement problem wrapped in an institutional one. The wellbeing programme at School A likely changes the *reporting rule*: pupils are told it's normal to name anxiety, given language for it, and perhaps a channel to report it. School B's streaming creates a different rule—sorting by ability—which may discourage admitting struggle, or push anxiety into other behaviours (absence, disruption, silence).

Before comparing levels, I'd want to know: same instrument, same timing, same anonymity? Who sees the data—teachers, parents, a researcher? In the irrigation systems I studied, farmers reported water theft differently when the monitor was a neighbour versus an outsider. Trust in the monitor changes the data.

Also: what happens *after* a pupil reports anxiety in each school? In Törbel's meadows, a rule without a graduated sanction was just talk. If School A's programme leads to support, and School B's streaming leads to labelling, the meaning of "high anxiety" diverges.

Are the pupil populations comparable—catchment, deprivation, special needs? I'd treat these as two distinct social-ecological systems, not two points on a single scale. The comparison only works if you understand the institutions generating the numbers.

You have an observation: companies that *chose* a four-day week report higher productivity a year later. You want the cause: the shorter week *made* them more productive.

First, we must distinguish what kind of claim this is. You are studying human organisations—like a polis, only the end is profit, not the good life. In such things we never get "always"; we get "for the most part." So the question is whether the four-day week is the *cause* of the rise, or whether the companies that can adopt it are already the kind that would rise anyway.

Four questions, as I would put them:

1. **What brought it about?** The decision to adopt. But who decides? Leadership with slack, or a culture that experiments. That same leadership may be why productivity rises.
2. **What is the thing?** "Productivity"—output per hour? Total output? Revenue per head? Measured by whom, and against what baseline?
3. **What is it made of?** The workforce, the processes, the industry. A software firm and a factory are not the same kind.
4. **What is it for?** The firms likely adopted it for retention, wellbeing, recruitment. Productivity may be a by-product, not the end.

If you only watch the adopters, you have no *control*—no similar firms that kept five days. You cannot tell whether productivity would have risen without the change. You also need to know the *order*: did output per hour rise first, or did hours drop and total output hold?

What would satisfy me: a comparison of matched firms, some adopting, some not, tracked before and after, with the mechanism spelled out—less burnout, fewer meetings, better focus. Until then, you have a plausible hypothesis, not a demonstration.

You have an observation: companies that chose a four-day week later report higher output per hour. You want to conclude the shorter week *caused* the gain. That is the step I would not take without a test.

The companies chose the change. Perhaps they were already improving, or had managers willing to experiment, or cut low-value work before the switch. The "report" comes from people with an interest in the policy looking successful. A year passes — markets shift, teams change, tools arrive. None of that is held steady.

If I wanted to know whether the shorter week itself raises productivity, I would not trust the volunteers' accounts. I would arrange two otherwise similar workplaces — same task, same people, same measures — and assign the shorter week to one by lot. Then watch the output week by week, measured the same way in both. If the gain appears only where the week was shortened, and persists when the schedule is swapped, the claim has teeth.

Without that arrangement, you have a story that fits the data, not a demonstration. What would it take to run such a test in your setting?

A familiar shape of argument. You see A followed by B and want to call A the cause of B. But look at what you actually observed: companies *that chose to adopt* a four-day week reported higher productivity a year later.

What you haven't observed: companies that wanted to but couldn't afford the experiment. Companies that tried it and quietly went back to five days. Companies that had a bad year, tried something new, and reverted to their mean — which they would have done anyway.

The firms that adopt a four-day week are already unusual: better managed, more secure, more willing to experiment. That selection does the work your causal claim wants to do.

If you want to convince me, show me what happened to the ones that *didn't* adopt it but were otherwise alike. Or show me a rollout where the timing was decided by something other than the firms themselves — a policy change, a staggered mandate, anything that breaks the self-selection.

Until then, you've got a conjunction. The necessity is something you've added.

That's a tempting pattern, but I'd worry it's the sort of favourable fact that slips into memory while the awkward ones vanish. Companies that *choose* a four-day week are already unusual — better resourced, better managed, more experimental. They're not a random draw.

My golden rule: whenever a published fact fits my conclusion too neatly, I write down the contrary case at once. Here the contrary cases are the firms that tried it and quietly went back to five days, or never reported, or folded. Without them, you're only measuring the survivors — like a pigeon fancier showing off his pouters and ignoring the squabs that died in the nest.

What would satisfy me: a natural history of the attempt. How many firms started? How many reverted, and why? Were productivity measures independent, or self-reported by the same people who championed the change? Did you match them to similar firms that didn't switch?

If you only have the volunteers who stayed and reported gains, you've got a selection experiment without a control — and I spent eight years on barnacles learning how treacherous that is.

That's not an argument. It's a selection effect wearing a causal label.

Companies that *choose* a four-day week are already unusual: better managed, better capitalized, more willing to experiment, probably already treating staff well enough that burnout isn't dragging them down. The productivity gain may come from all of that, not the shorter week.

Until you have that comparison, you have a press release, not a cause.

You have an association. You want a cause. That is the permanent problem.

Ask first: *which* companies adopted it? The ones with slack, with competent management, with workers who already trusted each other — or the desperate ones trying to stop a bleed? The "treatment" selects its own recipients. If the adopters were already on a different trajectory, the year-later figure tells you nothing about the policy.

Then ask what the change *meant* inside the firm. Did managers use the compressed week to cut meetings, automate drudgery, clarify priorities? Did workers reciprocate with intensity because they felt trusted? Or did they just sprint through the same waste in four days instead of five? The policy itself has no effect; only the responses to it do. Those responses depend on meanings you have not measured.

A proper comparison would track matched pairs — similar firms, similar starting points, one adopting, one not — and watch what actually changes in the daily organization of work. Even then you only get a local regularity, not a law.

So: the claim is plausible. The evidence you have does not support it. What would it take to get evidence that does?

That's a correlation. Companies that *chose* a four-day week are not a random sample. They're likely already better managed, in sectors where it's feasible, or running other experiments at the same time. The correlation tells you nothing about causation unless you can rule those out.
