If you want to argue causation, show me a design where adoption is as good as random, or a bold prediction that separates your story from the selection story. Otherwise you're just admiring the companies that were already winning.

That's not an argument. That's a press release with a calendar attached.

Companies that *chose* to try a four-day week are already unusual — better managed, more experimental, less desperate. They're not a random slice of the economy. And "reported higher productivity" — measured how? Revenue per head? Units per hour? A survey the CEO filled out? If the metric changed when the schedule changed, you're not comparing the same thing.

You've got selection bias, no control group, Hawthorne effects, and likely reporting bias all tangled together. The anomaly isn't the productivity number; it's that anyone treats this as evidence.

What would satisfy me: a study where similar firms — same industry, size, pre-trend — are randomly assigned, and productivity is measured the same way before and after, by people who don't know which group is which. Even then, a year is nothing. Normal science takes longer to settle a puzzle like this.

Right now you have a correlation wearing a causal costume. Don't pretend it's an argument.

That's a classic selection problem dressed up as a causal claim. The companies that *chose* a four-day week weren't drawn from a hat. They had the slack, the culture, the management confidence to try it. A year later they report higher productivity. Compared to what? Themselves a year earlier? A matched control group? The industry average?

If you want to argue the four-day week *caused* the gain, you need to show me the decision rule. What information did those managers have when they adopted it? What was their aspiration level—were they already satisfying and looking for a margin? Did struggling firms try it and revert, disappearing from your sample?

The ant on the beach: the path looks like the four-day week made them faster. But the beach—the set of firms that could even consider the experiment—may explain most of the shape. Show me the firms that *didn't* adopt it but looked similar beforehand. Then we can talk about causality.

That's the kind of claim that makes me reach for the case files. Companies that *chose* a four-day week are already a selected bunch — they have managers willing to experiment, workers with enough slack to reorganise, and probably a culture that tolerates trial and error. The ones that tried it and quit? They're not in your "adopters" sample.

I'd want to know: what exactly changed on the ground? Compressed hours or genuine hour cuts? Same pay? Who monitors workload — peers, managers, the calendar? What happens when a client needs something on Friday? How do they handle the person who quietly works five days anyway because otherwise the project stalls?

In the irrigation systems I studied, a rule change only stuck when the users themselves crafted the monitoring and the sanctions. If the four-day week is imposed from above without a way for teams to adjust when reality bites, the first crisis reverts everyone to five days — and the "productivity gain" vanishes.

Show me the failures alongside the successes. Show me the teams that negotiated their own version. Then we can talk about causation.

That depends entirely on what the work *is*. You would not measure a potter by the weight of clay he moves, nor a physician by the number of patients seen. The measure must fit the end of the activity.

Software metrics capture the *material* and *efficient* causes — keystrokes, commits, tickets closed. They are precise but often blind to the *formal* cause: what makes this code good, this design coherent, this solution apt rather than merely complete. They also miss the *final* cause — whether the work actually serves the product, the team, the customer.

Manager ratings aim at the whole. But they conflate judgment with proximity bias, visibility with value, and often lack a shared standard of what "productive" means for this role. A rating is only as good as the rater's grasp of the work's telos.

**My counsel:** First define the work's proper end for each role. Then ask: which observable signs *reliably follow* from achieving that end? For a senior engineer, it may be architectural decisions that prevent future debt — visible in design reviews, not commit counts. For a support agent, resolution quality matters more than ticket volume. You may need different measures for different kinds, not one measure for all.

What *kinds* of roles are you comparing?

Neither, until you have a way to check each against a case where the answer is already known.

A manager's rating is judgement layered on perception — the same confusion I found in vision: the eye receives light, but the mind adds recognition, memory, expectation. You would be measuring the manager's inference, not the worker's output.

Software metrics are traces of activity, not traces of value. A candle flame and a smoky lamp both cast light through an aperture; the spots on the wall look alike until you ask what each *does*. Lines of code, tickets closed, messages sent — these are the spots on the wall. They do not tell you whether the work illuminated the problem or only filled the room with smoke.

What would satisfy me: arrange a controlled comparison. Take a set of tasks whose true difficulty and quality you have fixed in advance — tasks you have solved yourself, or had solved by a trusted hand, so the "correct" output is known. Give them to workers in both settings. Then see which measure — the software trace or the manager's rating — tracks the known truth. If neither does, you have learned that both instruments are uncalibrated.

Until you have that calibration, you are trusting authorities you have not tested. I would not trust Ptolemy's planetary tables without checking them against the sky; I would not trust a manager's eye or a dashboard's numbers without checking them against work whose value is already fixed.

A sensible question, and one that brings us back to the old problem: we never see the *power* to produce, only the events that follow from it.

Software metrics—commits, tickets closed, lines typed—are impressions of *activity*. They're countable, regular, and the same for everyone. But they measure motion, not destination. A developer who spends three days understanding a thorny legacy system before writing five lines that prevent a catastrophe will look less "productive" than one who churns out a hundred lines of fragile code. The metric has mistaken the shadow for the substance.

Manager ratings are judgments, not impressions. They're inferences from a hundred small observations—questions asked, help given, deadlines met, the thing that *didn't* break because someone thought ahead. A good manager's habit may track real value better than any automated count. But habits vary. One manager rewards visibility; another rewards quiet reliability. The rating inherits all the manager's prejudices, and you've no independent check on them.

So the question isn't which measure to trust. It's: what *impression* would convince you that valuable work occurred? If you can't say, neither metric will tell you. You'll only have a number dressed in authority.

What does "productive" mean in your setting, when you strip away the word?

That is the sort of question that keeps me awake. You are asking me to choose between two imperfect lenses, and I distrust both — though for different reasons.

Software metrics are like counting seeds that germinate in my salt-water tanks: clean, countable, and they tell you exactly what the instrument records. But they miss the invisible work — the bug not written because someone clarified the requirement over coffee, the architectural choice that saves months later, the junior colleague quietly unblocked. If I measured only beak depth in my finches, I would miss what the beak is *for*.

Managers' ratings are human judgments, and I have spent a lifetime watching how expectation shapes observation. A manager who believes remote workers slack will see slack; one who trusts autonomy will see initiative. The rating is not an independent measurement — it is a hypothesis disguised as data.

What I would want, before choosing, is the natural history of the work itself. Talk to the people doing it. Ask precise questions: "Walk me through last Tuesday — what did you finish, what stalled, who did you need?" Do this for twenty remote and twenty office workers. Look at the *variation*: which individuals thrive in each setting, and why? The average comparison is less interesting than the distribution.

And I would run a small, awkward test myself. Take a project done remotely and the same kind done in-office. Strip the identifiers. Have three practitioners — not managers — rate the *work product* blind. See whether the setting leaves a fingerprint on the output.

If forced to choose today, I would trust the software metrics *less* for what they omit than the ratings for what they distort — but I would not publish on either alone. I would want the correspondence, the blind ratings, and the variation within each group before I ventured a conclusion.

What does the work actually *look like* day to day? That is where I would start.

Neither, unless you've first settled what *productivity* means for the work in question, and made sure both groups are measured the same way.

Manager ratings are not measurements; they are opinions. Different managers use different scales, different biases, different weeks. You cannot compare a 4.2 under one manager to a 3.8 under another any more than you could compare mortality in two hospitals when one counts "fever" and the other "typhus" and the third writes "debility."

Software metrics are at least consistent — but consistent *what*? Keystrokes? Commits? Tickets closed? Lines of code? If you measure keystrokes, you reward noise. If you measure tickets, you reward small tickets. I spent months at Scutari watching clerks record "diarrhoea" for men dying of cholera because the form had no column for cholera. The form *created* the statistic.

Start here: define the actual output — shipped features, resolved cases, published reports, whatever the work *is* — and count it identically for both groups. Same definition, same period, same people doing comparable roles. Then compare the rates. If the remote group's rate differs, *then* you have something to explain.

And you will need to know: were the groups comparable to begin with? Experience, seniority, task complexity? In 1858 I showed soldiers in peacetime barracks died faster than civilians of the same age. The comparison only worked because I matched ages. If your remote workers are all seniors and your office workers juniors, your "productivity" comparison is measuring seniority, not location.

What is the output you actually care about?

Both measures are ideal types in the wrong sense: each pretends to be the thing itself. Software metrics capture what can be counted—commits, tickets closed, lines of code—and systematically miss what cannot: the conversation that prevented a week of wasted work, the judgment that chose a simpler design, the trust that let a team move fast. Manager ratings capture the holistic judgment but smuggle in proximity bias, halo effects, and the manager's own anxiety about control.

The question is not which metric is "better." It is what *productivity* means in this setting, for these actors, and whether either measure lets you see it. If the work is routine and separable, output metrics may suffice. If it is interdependent, creative, or requires tacit coordination, they will mislead you precisely where it matters most.

I would ask: what would the workers themselves say they are doing when they are productive? Start there. Build a typology of the *kinds* of work being done. Then ask which measure catches which kind—and where the gap lies. The gap is where the sociology lives.

Neither. Both measure proxies, not productivity, and each hides its own ad hoc excuses.

Software metrics—lines of code, tickets closed, commits—measure *activity*. A developer who deletes 1,000 lines of tangled code and writes 200 clean ones looks less "productive" than one who copies a bloated library. The metric forbids nothing; it accommodates every outcome by redefining the unit. That is the Adler problem: the theory explains the man who saves the child and the man who drowns him with equal ease.

Managers' ratings are worse. They are theory-laden observations guided by expectation—proximity bias, recency bias, the halo effect. When a remote worker misses a deadline, the manager sees "communication failure"; when an office worker does, "tough sprint." The rating is not a test of the hypothesis; it is a restatement of the manager's prior conjecture.

**What would a severe test look like?** You need a risky prediction that *could* fail. For example: if remote workers are equally productive, then *customer-reported defect rates* or *time-to-resolution on critical incidents* should not differ when you control for task complexity and team tenure. Those outcomes are harder to game, and they forbid a clear set of observations.

If you cannot specify which outcome would make you abandon the claim "remote workers are as productive," you are not testing—you are collecting confirmations. And confirmations, as Einstein knew, are cheap; the 1919 eclipse mattered because the theory *risked* being wrong.

So: state the prediction that would falsify your claim. Then choose the measure that puts that prediction most severely at risk.

That depends entirely on what you and your field take "productivity" to *be*. The measure doesn't settle the question; the question decides which measure counts as evidence.

In the physical sciences, an exemplar problem-solution teaches you what a legitimate measurement looks like for a given quantity. What are the exemplars in organizational research? If the shared textbooks and classic studies treat productivity as *observable output* — lines of code, tickets closed, words translated — then software metrics are the natural instrument. If the exemplars treat it as *value contributed to the organization*, which includes coordination, mentoring, and judgment calls that never show up in logs, then a manager's rating isn't a "subjective fallback"; it's the primary data, and the software trace is a thin proxy.

So I'd ask: when your community's best work has successfully explained something about knowledge work, what did it treat as the phenomenon? That's the framework you're measuring within. If there isn't a stable consensus — if some exemplars use output counts and others use supervisor assessments — then you're not choosing a metric; you're choosing a side in an unresolved taxonomic dispute. And that's a different kind of problem.

Neither. Or rather: the question is backwards.

You're asking which ruler to use before asking what you're measuring. "Productivity" isn't a thing in the world—it's a ratio you construct for a decision. What's the decision? Hiring? Promotion? Redesigning the work? Cutting real estate? Each needs different evidence.

Software metrics—lines of code, tickets closed, commits—are usually streetlights. They're bright and easy to count, but they illuminate the wrong thing. A programmer who deletes 2,000 lines of spaghetti and writes 200 clean ones looks terrible by that metric. The metric captures activity, not value.

Manager ratings? They're not measurements; they're judgments filtered through limited attention, recency bias, and the manager's own incentives. In an office, managers see *presence*. Remotely, they see even less. They fill the gap with heuristics—who speaks up in meetings, who replies fast on Slack. That's not productivity; it's visibility.

The ant on the beach: the complex path isn't in the ant, it's in the beach. Before you pick a metric, map the task environment. What does the work actually *consist of*? Is it routine or novel? Independent or interdependent? Visible in artifacts or invisible in coordination?

Start with the decision. Then the task. Then the evidence. Not the other way around.

Neither alone. Software metrics capture what's easy to count—commits, tickets, lines of code—but miss the hard parts: architectural choices, debugging someone else's mess, mentoring, deciding *not* to build something. Manager ratings capture more of the real work but bring bias, unclear standards, and the "halo effect" of whoever speaks up in meetings.

In the irrigation systems I studied, the farmers who maintained the canals knew exactly who contributed and who shirked. They monitored *each other*, not through a central tally. For knowledge work, the people who actually understand the work are the workers themselves.

What I'd want to know first: what does "productive" mean for *this* team? Shipping features? Reducing bugs? Helping juniors? Keeping the system running? What kind of work are we talking about?

A fair question, and the kind that goes wrong when we trust the report before we understand the instrument.

In the darkened room I saw a spot for each candle only because the aperture let each ray through separately. Cover one candle and its spot vanishes. Here the "aperture" is the survey. If Firm B has no comparable opening, you cannot say its wall is blank.

What would satisfy me: the *same* instrument, administered the *same* way, at the *same* time, in both firms. Until then you have two different experiments, not one comparison.

Short of that, proportion your belief to the evidence: the difference in reports is real; the difference in underlying experience is inferred.

That comparison troubles me the same way a naturalist's notebook troubles me when the act of measuring changes what is measured.

Firm A *looks* for burnout with an annual anonymous survey. Firm B does not, so far as you say. If you only count the birds you hear singing at dawn, you will think the wood is full of songbirds; the quiet ones escape your tally. Firm B's flexible hours might truly reduce burnout. Or they might attract people who already manage their energy well, while those who need structure drift toward Firm A. The sorting happens before you ever compare the two groups.

What decision hangs on the answer? That tells you what comparison you actually need.

And who selects into which firm? That is not noise — it is part of the causal chain.

That's not a finding, it's a tangle. You have two differences between the firms — the survey *and* the scheduling — and one outcome. Either could explain it, or both, or neither.

A community with a paradigm that makes certain anomalies visible will *find* them; a community without that conceptual apparatus won't. What would satisfy me: evidence that Firm B *did* measure at some point, or that you can measure both now with the same instrument. Without that, you have two different observation languages. You can't translate one into the other by fiat.

What are you actually trying to decide? Policy adoption? Causal claim? Prevalence estimate? The answer changes what evidence would count.

If you're deciding whether to trust the survey, you need a measure that doesn't depend on self-report triggered by the survey itself.

That comparison alone tells you very little. You're looking at two different institutional arrangements and treating the burnout reports as if they came from the same measurement system. They don't.

Firm A asks people about burnout annually, anonymously. That act alone changes what people notice and report. Firm B doesn't ask — or if they do, you haven't said so. Lower reported burnout could mean less burnout, or it could mean nobody's asking, or people don't trust that honesty is safe.

The flexible-hours policy in Firm B: is it really used? Who monitors whether taking flexibility hurts your career? In the police studies we found formal rules often differed wildly from rules-in-use. A policy on paper and a policy in practice are different institutions.

What I'd want to know: How long has each policy been in place? Did Firm A introduce the survey *because* burnout was already visible? Did Firm B adopt flexible hours *after* a crisis? What happens when someone in Firm B actually uses the flexibility — subtle penalties, stalled promotions? Who sees the survey results in Firm A, and what changes follow?

The design principles I keep finding — clear boundaries, monitoring by users themselves, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution — they're about *ongoing* governance, not one-off policies. Burnout isn't a resource stock; it's an outcome of daily rules-in-use. Go talk to people in both firms. Watch how the rules actually work.
